newsitem.title: USA: Read-Rite rejects Applied Magnetics offer.
newsitem.headline: Read-Rite rejects Applied Magnetics offer.

text.p: Read-Rite Corp. said Monday it rejected an unsolicited takeover bid worth $1.76 billion from Applied Magnetics Corp., another maker of computer disk drives.
The combined companies would have $1.8 billion in annual sales and equity worth $3.4 billion.
Read-Rite, the world's largest independent supplier of recording heads, said its board of directors voted unanimously to reject the offer and remain independent.

"Read-Rite's independence has been critical to its success to date, and we are confident that adherence to our existing, long-term strategic business plan will enable us to deliver further value to our shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, and the company's other constituencies in the future," said Cyril Yansouni, chairman and chief executive.
In February, Applied Magnetics offered 0.679 share of its common stock, worth about $36, for each Read-Rite share.
Read-Rite, based in Milpitas, Calif., said it hired Goldman, Sachs & Co. as its independent financial adviser.
Yansouni said in an interview that Applied Magnetics' hostile bid followed an earlier proposal from Applied Magnetics to be taken over by Read-Rite.
By contrast, Applied Magnetics has said only that it was seeking a friendly merger agreement.

"We have not had serious discussions in nine months, though we had a bit more in-depth talks in the past month. They were the calling party, and the topic of discussion was for us to acquire them," Yansouni said in an interview soon after Read-Rite rejected the deal.
"We don't see anything that they bring to us."
He added that Applied Magnetics wanted a merger to compensate for its lack of investment in the next generation of computer disk-drive technology.
Yansouni said the Applied Magnetics takeover talks "were for information purposes" and declined to say if any terms had been discussed.
An Applied spokesman was not immediately available to comment on Yansouni's statements.
Read-Rite's stock edged up 6.25 cents to $30.75 on Nasdaq. Goleta, Calif.-based Applied Magnetics jumped $4.25 to $43.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Based on the ratio and Applied Magnetic's current stock price, the offer values Read-Rite at a discount of about $28.35 a share.

"Wall Street made up its mind (about the bid) and it made our job easier. But our decision was not based on (the offer) price," Yansouni said. "The decision was based on the continued huge potential for our company as we execute our game plan."

Since the bid was announced, Applied Magnetic's stock has fallen about 22 percent, including a partial rebound on Monday. Read-Rite stock has shed 3.5 percent during a period in which the Dow Jones industrial average slid 2.15 percent and the Nasdaq composite dropped 3 percent.

Yansouni said Read-Rite's "huge potential" lies in its investment in the production of magneto-resistance disk-drive heads. The next-generation technology -- Applied's weak point -- would supplant current products by 1998, he said.

"The disk drive industry is moving to magneto-resistance. In the December quarter, 17 percent of our production was of this type and this quarter it will be in excess of 20 percent. Applied has not invested in this technology and that is why we think they want to do this," Yansouni said.
Read-Rite aims to have magneto-resistance heads account for "half or more" of total manufactuing output by the end of calendar year 1997, he said.
